methodological_rigor.justification: The cross-sectional observational design is appropriate for the descriptive aims (ownership, use, willingness), but the analysis relies exclusively on separate univariate logistic regressions without any multivariable adjustment, so the reported associations (education, income, marital status, BMI, employment, MVPA) are confounded with each other given overlapping socioeconomic constructs. No a priori power calculation is reported, and no correction for the many simultaneous tests across three outcomes and roughly 15 predictors is applied despite the p<0.05 threshold. Participants are drawn from a single health system (Northwestern Medicine EDW) with a predominantly White, highly educated, high-income, smartphone-owning sample, introducing substantial selection bias that the authors acknowledge but cannot mitigate. Missing data handling is limited to complete-case analysis (518/736), and self-report is the sole data source for both exposures and outcomes.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a single cross-sectional self-report survey of 518 post-treatment cancer survivors from one US health system, which maps to Oxford CEBM level 4 (cross-sectional/low-quality cohort evidence on prevalence and correlates). Clinical relevance is moderate: the topic (mHealth adoption and data-sharing willingness in survivorship) is practically important and the Discussion offers actionable integration strategies (EHR vendor partnerships, dashboards, equity scaffolding), but the endpoints are surrogate behavioral/attitudinal measures rather than patient-centered outcomes like OS, PFS, QoL, or validated PA change. The findings refine descriptive estimates of ownership prevalence but do not inform guidelines, change practice, or demonstrate downstream clinical benefit.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the applicable checklist for this cross-sectional observational study. Core items are present: eligibility criteria are enumerated, setting and recruitment window (April to June 2023 via NMEDW) are stated, measures and operationalization of predictors/outcomes are described, and sample flow (759 consented, 736 completed, 518 complete-case) is reported in text. However, no flow diagram is provided, no bias assessment section is included, missing-data handling is not described beyond complete-case analysis, no sensitivity analyses are reported, and no sample size justification is given. The manuscript contains no data-availability or code-availability statement; the measures are standard but the dataset and STATA code are not shared or referenced in a repository.

novelty_literature.justification: The work is incremental empirical novelty in the population dimension: it updates mHealth ownership/use prevalence estimates in post-treatment survivors using 2023 data and reports slightly higher wearable ownership (52.9%) than the 2020 to 2021 HINTS-based studies by Zhou and Gitonga that the authors directly cite as comparators. No new conceptual framework, no new instrument, no new analytic method, and no underserved population is targeted (the sample is predominantly White, educated, higher-income). The correlates identified (education, income, age, BMI, PA engagement) replicate well-established patterns in the connected-health literature the authors themselves reference.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written and logically organized, with a tight Introduction, well-structured Methods, Results that mirror the three outcomes, and a comprehensive Discussion. The abstract is self-contained and quantitatively anchored (97.5% smartphone ownership, 52.9% tracker ownership, 32.4% app use, 64.3% willing to share) and accurately reflects the main findings. The Discussion is somewhat long and partially redundant where it enumerates integration strategies (dashboards, alerts, remote monitoring) that go well beyond what the data support. Table captions are extremely sparse (just titles) and would be hard to interpret standalone.

key_strengths: Reasonably sized (n=518), well-characterized survivor sample from a single large health system with a defined recruitment window and clear eligibility criteria
Disaggregates specific device/app brands (Apple Watch, Fitbit, MyFitnessPal, Peloton) rather than only aggregate ownership, adding texture to the descriptive picture
Updates prevalence estimates post-pandemic (2023) and situates them against HINTS-based comparators (Zhou, Gitonga)
Clearly written abstract and logically organized sections, with a thoughtful equity-focused discussion of implementation strategies
key_concerns: Analysis is restricted to separate univariate logistic regressions with no multivariable adjustment and no multiplicity correction, so correlates (education, income, marital status, BMI, employment, MVPA) are mutually confounded
No power calculation, no sensitivity analyses, and complete-case-only handling of the 736 to 518 attrition without characterizing the excluded participants
Single-center, predominantly White, highly educated, high-income, smartphone-owning sample materially limits generalizability, especially for conclusions about equity and underserved populations
Low Oxford level of evidence (4) with surrogate behavioral/attitudinal outcomes rather than clinical endpoints; findings are descriptive and incremental over prior HINTS analyses
No data-availability or code statement; STATA scripts and the questionnaire-level dataset are not shared
Discussion speculates extensively about EHR dashboards, nudges, and remote monitoring workflows that are not supported by the study's data
chief_reviewer.rationale: Correctly conducted but narrowly scoped descriptive survey with univariate-only analysis, a non-representative single-site sample, and incremental novelty relative to published HINTS analyses; appropriate for a Tier 4 outlet after minor revisions clarifying statistical limitations and tempering the integration-focused discussion.
